{{Short description|Theorem on the equality of analytic functions}}
In [[real analysis]] and [[complex analysis]], branches of [[mathematics]], the '''identity theorem''' for [[analytic function]]s states: given functions ''f'' and ''g'' analytic on a [[Domain (mathematical analysis)|domain]] ''D'' (open and connected subset of <math>\mathbb{R}</math> or <math>\mathbb{C}</math>), if ''f'' = ''g'' on some <math>S \subseteq D</math>, where <math>S </math> has an [[accumulation point]] in ''D'', then ''f'' = ''g'' on ''D''.<ref>For real functions, see {{cite book |first=Steven G. |last=Krantz |first2=Harold R. |last2=Parks |title=A Primer of Real Analytic Functions |edition=Second |publisher=Birkhäuser |location=Boston |year=2002 |isbn=0-8176-4264-1 |at=Corollary 1.2.7 }}</ref> 

Thus an analytic function is completely determined by its values on a single open neighborhood in ''D'', or even a countable subset of ''D'' with an accumulation point (provided this contains a converging sequence together with its limit). This is not true in general for real-differentiable functions, even [[smoothness|infinitely real-differentiable functions]]. In comparison, analytic functions are a much more rigid notion.

The underpinning fact from which the theorem is established is the [[Analyticity of holomorphic functions|expandability of a holomorphic function into its Taylor series]].

The connectedness assumption on the domain ''D'' is necessary. For example, if ''D'' consists of two disjoint [[open sets]], <math>f</math> can be <math>0</math> on one open set, and <math>1</math> on another, while <math>g</math> is <math>0</math> on one, and <math>2</math> on another.

== Lemma ==

If two holomorphic functions <math> f </math> and <math> g </math> on a domain ''D'' agree on a set S which has an accumulation point <math>c</math> in <math>D</math>, then <math>f = g </math> on a disk in <math>D</math> centered at <math>c</math>.

To prove this, it is enough to show that <math>f^{(n)}(c)= g^{(n)}(c)</math> for all <math>n\geq 0</math>, since both functions are analytic.

If this is not the case, let <math> m </math> be the smallest nonnegative [[integer]] with <math>f^{(m)}(c)\ne g^{(m)}(c)</math>. By holomorphy, we have the following Taylor series representation in some open neighborhood U of <math> c </math>:

:<math>
\begin{align}
(f - g)(z) &{}=(z - c)^m  \cdot \left[\frac{(f - g)^{(m)}(c)}{m!} + \frac{(z - c) \cdot (f - g)^{(m+1)}(c)}{(m+1)!} + \cdots  \right]  \\[6pt]  
           &{}=(z - c)^m  \cdot h(z).
\end{align}
</math>

By continuity, <math> h </math> is non-zero in some small open disk <math> B</math> around <math>c</math>. But then <math>f-g\neq 0</math> on the punctured set <math>B-\{c\}</math>. This contradicts the assumption that <math>c</math> is an accumulation point of <math>\{f = g\}</math>.

This lemma shows that for a complex number <math> a \in \mathbb{C}</math>, the [[fiber (mathematics)|fiber]] <math>f^{-1}(a)</math>  is a discrete (and therefore countable) set, unless <math>f \equiv a</math>.

== Proof ==

Define the set on which <math>f</math> and <math>g</math> have the same [[Taylor series|Taylor expansion]]:
<math display="block">T = \left\{ z \in D \mathrel{\Big\vert} f^{(k)}(z) = g^{(k)}(z) \text{ for all } k \geq 0\right\} = \bigcap_{k=0}^\infty \left\{ z \in D \mathrel{\Big\vert} \bigl(f^{(k)}- g^{(k)}\bigr)(z) = 0\right\}.</math>

We'll show <math>T</math> is nonempty, [[Clopen set|open, and closed]]. Then by [[Connected space|connectedness]] of <math>D</math>, <math>T</math> must be all of <math>D</math>, which implies <math>f=g</math> on <math>T=D</math>.

By the lemma, <math>f = g</math> in a disk centered at <math>c</math> in <math>D</math>, they have the same Taylor series at <math>c</math>, so <math>c\in T</math>, hence <math>T</math> is nonempty.

As <math>f</math> and <math>g</math> are holomorphic on <math>D</math>, <math>\forall w\in T</math>, the Taylor series of <math>f</math> and <math>g</math> at <math>w</math> have non-zero [[radius of convergence]]. Therefore, the open disk <math>B_r(w)</math> also lies in <math>T</math> for some <math>r</math>. So <math>T</math> is open.

By holomorphy of <math>f</math> and <math>g</math>, they have holomorphic derivatives, so all <math>\textstyle f^{(n)}, g^{(n)}</math> are continuous. This means that <math>\textstyle \bigl\{z \in D \mathrel{\big\vert} \bigl(f^{(k)} - g^{(k)}\bigr)(z) = 0\bigr\}</math> is closed for all <math>k</math>. <math>S</math> is an intersection of closed sets, so it's closed.

== Full characterisation ==

Since the identity theorem is concerned with the equality of two [[Holomorphic function|holomorphic functions]], we can simply consider the difference (which remains holomorphic) and can simply characterise when a holomorphic function is identically <math display="inline">0</math>. The following result can be found in.<ref name="lex2s476">{{Cite book
| title=Lexikon der Mathematik
| language=de
| volume=2
| publisher=Springer Spektrum Verlag
| editor=Guido Walz
| place=Mannheim
| year=2017
| pages=476
| isbn=978-3-662-53503-5}}</ref>

=== Claim ===
Let <math display="inline">G\subseteq\mathbb{C}</math> denote a non-empty, [[connectedness|connected]] open subset of the [[complex plane]].
For analytic <math display="inline">h:G\to\mathbb{C}</math> the following are equivalent.

# <math display="inline">h\equiv 0</math> on <math display="inline">G</math>;
# the set <math display="inline">G_{0}=\{z\in G\mid h(z)=0\}</math> contains an [[Limit point of a set|accumulation point]], <math display="inline">z_{0}</math>;
# the set <math display="inline">G_{\ast}=\bigcap_{n\in\N_0} G_{n}</math> is non-empty, where <math display="inline">G_{n} := \{z\in G\mid h^{(n)}(z)=0\}</math>.

=== Proof ===

'''(1 <math display="inline">\Rightarrow</math> 2)''' holds trivially.

'''(2 <math display="inline">\Rightarrow</math> 3)''' is shown in section ''Lemma'' in part with Taylor expansion at accumulation point, just substitute ''g=0''. 

'''(3 <math display="inline">\Rightarrow</math> 1)''' is shown in section ''Proof'' with set where all derivatives of ''f-g'' vanishes, just substitute ''g=0''.

[[Q.E.D.]]
